sub_modules.title: DNA Structure, Topology & Chromatin Packaging
sub_modules.overview: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) stores genetic information in an antiparallel, right-handed double helix whose topological state and histone-mediated compaction govern genome accessibility.

core_concepts.heading: Discovery, Double-Helix Geometry & Helical Polymorphism
core_concepts.theory: Following Griffith's transformation experiments (1928), Avery-MacLeod-McCarty (1944), and Hershey-Chase (1952), Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins (1953) elucidated the B-DNA double helix. Two antiparallel polydeoxyribonucleotide strands (5'->3' and 3'->5') coil around a common axis, held together by Watson-Crick hydrogen bonds (A=T with 2 H-bonds; G≡C with 3 H-bonds) and hydrophobic π-π base-stacking interactions.
key_principles: Chargaff's Parity Rules: In any double-stranded DNA molecule, [A] = [T], [G] = [C], and total purines ([A]+[G]) equal total pyrimidines ([T]+[C]). Higher GC% increases thermal melting temperature (Tm) due to three H-bonds and stronger dipole base-stacking.

Major vs. Minor Grooves: Asymmetric glycosidic bond angles create a wide Major Groove (2.2 nm, rich in sequence-specific H-bond donors/acceptors read by transcription factors) and a narrow Minor Groove (1.2 nm, bound by architectural proteins like TBP and Hoechst dyes).

A, B, and Z Helical Conformations: Physiological B-DNA is right-handed (10.5 bp/turn, 0.34 nm rise, C2'-endo sugar pucker). Dehydrated A-DNA and DNA-RNA hybrids are wider and right-handed (11 bp/turn, 0.26 nm rise, C3'-endo pucker). Alternating purine-pyrimidine sequences (e.g., poly dG-dC) under high salt or negative supercoiling adopt left-handed Z-DNA (12 bp/turn, zig-zag backbone, syn-G / anti-C).

core_concepts.heading: DNA Topology, Supercoiling & Topoisomerases
core_concepts.theory: In covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA in plasmids, bacteria, mitochondria) or loop-anchored eukaryotic chromosomal domains, the two strands cannot be separated without altering the topological Linking Number (Lk), which partitions into helical Twist (Tw) and superhelical Writhe (Wr).
key_principles: Topological Conservation (Lk = Tw + Wr): Lk is strictly an integer that can only change if one or both phosphodiester backbones are broken. Most cellular DNA is maintained in an underwound, negatively supercoiled state (ΔLk < 0, σ ≈ -0.06) to facilitate strand separation during replication and transcription.

Type I vs. Type II Topoisomerases: Type I topoisomerases cleave one strand of DNA, changing Lk in steps of ±1 without ATP (except reverse gyrase). Type II topoisomerases (including bacterial DNA Gyrase and eukaryotic Topo IIα) cleave both strands, pass an intact duplex through the gate using ATP hydrolysis, and change Lk in steps of ±2.

core_concepts.heading: Nucleosomes, Histone Octamers & Higher-Order Chromatin
core_concepts.theory: A human diploid nucleus packs ~2 meters of linear DNA (6.4 × 10^9 bp) into a ~10 μm nucleus via hierarchical chromatin folding.
key_principles: The Nucleosome Core Particle (11 nm 'Beads-on-a-String'): 147 bp of negatively charged DNA wraps 1.65 times in a left-handed toroidal superhelix around a positively charged (Lys/Arg-rich) core histone octamer composed of two H2A–H2B dimers and one (H3–H4)2 tetramer.

Linker Histone H1 & Solenoid/Zig-Zag Compaction: Histone H1 binds the ~20–60 bp linker DNA at the entry/exit dyad axis, compacting the 11 nm fiber into 30 nm chromatin fibers, Cohesin/CTCF-mediated loops (300 nm), and Condensin-driven mitotic chromosomes (1,400 nm).

sub_modules.title: DNA Replication Mechanics, Replisome Enzymology & Proofreading
sub_modules.overview: Semiconservative DNA replication (Meselson and Stahl, 1958) duplicates the genome with an error rate below 10^-9 per base pair through coordinated origin licensing, bidirectional unwinding, asymmetric strand synthesis, and exonucleolytic proofreading.

core_concepts.heading: Origin Recognition, Unwinding & The Replisome Trombone Model
core_concepts.theory: Because all known DNA polymerases synthesize exclusively in the 5'->3' direction and require a pre-existing 3'-OH primer terminus, antiparallel templates force semidiscontinuous replication: the Leading Strand is synthesized continuously toward the fork, while the Lagging Strand is synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (1000–2000 nt in bacteria; 100–200 nt in eukaryotes).
key_principles: Origin Recognition & Licensing: In E. coli, DnaA-ATP binds oriC 9-mer/13-mer repeats to melt AT-rich DNA and load the hexameric DnaB helicase (via DnaC). In eukaryotes, the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) recruits Cdc6 and Cdt1 in G1 phase to load the double-hexameric MCM2–7 helicase; S-CDK and DDK phosphorylate MCM to activate the CMG helicase complex once per cell cycle.

Unwinding & Single-Strand Protection: Helicase unwinds the duplex using ATP, generating positive supercoils ahead of the fork (relieved by DNA Gyrase / Topo II). Single-Strand Binding proteins (SSB in prokaryotes; RPA in eukaryotes) coat ssDNA to prevent hairpin re-annealing and nuclease attack.

Priming & Polymerase Switching: Primase (DnaG in bacteria; DNA Pol α–primase in eukaryotes) synthesizes a short ~8–12 nt RNA primer. In eukaryotes, RFC (clamp loader) loads the trimeric PCNA sliding clamp, triggering a switch from low-processivity Pol α to high-processivity Pol ε (leading strand) and Pol δ (lagging strand).

core_concepts.heading: Okazaki Maturation, Fidelity Proofreading & Telomere End-Replication
core_concepts.theory: High-fidelity genome duplication requires three serial fidelity filters—base selection (10^-4–10^-5), 3'->5' exonuclease proofreading (10^-2), and post-replicative mismatch repair (10^-2–10^-3)—plus specialized reverse transcription at linear chromosome ends.
key_principles: Okazaki Fragment Maturation: In bacteria, DNA Pol I uses its 5'->3' exonuclease (nick translation) to remove RNA primers and fill gaps. In eukaryotes, Pol δ displaces the RNA primer into a flap cleaved by Flap Endonuclease 1 (FEN1) and RNase H; DNA Ligase I seals the nick using ATP (or NAD+ in bacteria) via an AMP-lysine intermediate.

3'->5' Exonucleolytic Proofreading: If an incorrect tautomer or mismatched dNTP is incorporated, the frayed 3'-OH terminus cannot translocate in the polymerase active site and shifts to the 3'->5' exonuclease site for hydrolytic excision.

The End-Replication Problem & Telomerase: Removal of the terminal 5' RNA primer on the lagging strand leaves a 3' single-stranded overhang (TTAGGG repeats in vertebrates). Telomerase (TERT reverse transcriptase + TERC intrinsic RNA template) extends the 3' overhang so Pol α/δ can complete the complementary C-rich strand.

sub_modules.title: RNA Biology: Transcription, Splicing & Functional Non-Coding RNAs
sub_modules.overview: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) bridges static genomic storage and dynamic cellular execution through coding transcripts (mRNA), catalytic ribozymes (rRNA, snRNA), adaptor molecules (tRNA), and regulatory non-coding networks (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA).

core_concepts.heading: RNA Polymerases, Co-Transcriptional Processing & Spliceosome Mechanics
core_concepts.theory: Unlike DNA polymerases, RNA polymerases initiate de novo synthesis (5'->3') without a primer. While prokaryotes use a single core RNA Polymerase (α2ββ'ω) directed by σ-factors (e.g., σ70 binding -35 TTGACA and -10 TATAAT Pribnow boxes), eukaryotes divide labor across three nuclear polymerases: RNA Pol I (28S, 18S, 5.8S rRNA), RNA Pol II (all mRNAs, miRNAs, most snRNAs), and RNA Pol III (tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA).
key_principles: RNA Pol II CTD Phosphorylation Code: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of Rpb1 contains heptad repeats (YSPTSPS; 52 in humans). TFIIH phosphorylates Ser5 at promoter clearance to recruit 5' capping enzymes; P-TEFb phosphorylates Ser2 during productive elongation to recruit splicing and 3' polyadenylation factors.

5' Capping & 3' Polyadenylation: Nascent pre-mRNA receives a 5' 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap via an unusual 5'-5' triphosphate linkage (protects from 5' exonucleases and binds eIF4E). At the 3' end, CPSF and CstF recognize the AAUAAA poly(A) signal, cleave the transcript, and Poly(A) Polymerase (PAP) adds ~200–250 adenines without a template.

Pre-mRNA Splicing (Two Transesterifications): The Spliceosome (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNPs) excises introns with 5'-GU and 3'-AG boundaries. First, the 2'-OH of the conserved intronic Branchpoint Adenine (bound by U2) attacks the 5' splice site, forming a 2'-5' phosphodiester lariat. Second, the freed 3'-OH of Exon 1 attacks the 3' splice site, joining the exons and releasing the intron lariat (catalyzed by the U2/U6 RNA ribozyme active site).

core_concepts.heading: Coding vs. Non-Coding RNA Classes & RNA Interference (RNAi)
core_concepts.theory: Only ~1.5% of the human genome encodes protein, whereas >75% is transcribed into functional non-coding RNAs that regulate translation, chromatin architecture, and transposon silencing.
key_principles: Structural & Catalytic RNAs (rRNA, tRNA, snRNA, snoRNA): rRNA forms the peptidyl transferase ribozyme core of the ribosome; tRNA adopts an L-shaped 3D cloverleaf (D-loop, anticodon loop, TΨC loop, 3'-CCA acceptor stem); snoRNAs guide 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation of rRNA.

miRNA vs. siRNA (RISC Silencing): Primary miRNAs (pri-miRNAs) are cleaved in the nucleus by Drosha/DGCR8 into pre-miRNA hairpins, exported by Exportin-5, and diced in the cytoplasm by Dicer (an RNase III enzyme) into ~21–22 bp duplexes. Loaded into Argonaute (Ago) within RISC: perfect complementarity (typical of exogenous dsRNA-derived siRNAs) triggers endonucleolytic mRNA cleavage ('slicing'), whereas partial seed-region complementarity (typical of animal miRNAs at 3' UTRs) causes translational repression and deadenylation.

Long Non-Coding RNAs (lncRNAs >200 nt): Act as molecular scaffolds, decoys, and epigenetic guides—canonically exemplified by XIST, which coats the inactive X chromosome in female mammals to recruit Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2).

sub_modules.title: Protein Synthesis: Genetic Code, tRNA Charging & Ribosome Mechanics
sub_modules.overview: Translation decodes mRNA nucleotide triplets (codons) into a polypeptide chain (N-terminus to C-terminus) at a rate of 15–20 amino acids/sec in bacteria and 3–6 amino acids/sec in eukaryotes.

core_concepts.heading: The Genetic Code, Wobble Pairing & Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetases
core_concepts.theory: The genetic code consists of 64 triplet codons ($4^3$): 61 sense codons especificar 20 standard amino acids (plus selenocysteine at UGA and pyrrolysine at UAG in specialized contexts) and 3 stop codons (UAA ochre, UAG amber, UGA opal). The code is degenerate, unambiguous, non-overlapping, and nearly universal.
key_principles: Crick's Wobble Hypothesis: The 1st and 2nd codon bases form strict Watson-Crick pairs with the 3rd and 2nd anticodon positions, but the 3rd codon base (3' end) can form non-standard 'wobble' hydrogen bonds with the 1st anticodon base (5' end, often modified to Inosine [I], which pairs with U, C, or A). This allows ~32–45 tRNAs to decode all 61 sense codons.

Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetase (aaRS) Activation ('The Second Genetic Code'): There are 20 distinct aaRS enzymes (1 per amino acid). Charging consumes 2 high-energy phosphate bonds: Step 1 activates the amino acid carboxyl group with ATP to form aminoacyl-AMP + PPi (followed by pyrophosphatase hydrolysis of PPi -> 2 Pi); Step 2 transfers the aminoacyl group to the 2'- or 3'-OH of the tRNA 3'-CCA adenosine. Editing pockets hydrolyze misacylated amino acids (e.g., IleRS rejecting Val).

core_concepts.heading: Initiation, Elongation (A/P/E Sites) & Termination Energetics
core_concepts.theory: Ribosomes (70S = 30S + 50S in prokaryotes; 80S = 40S + 60S in eukaryotes) contain three tRNA-binding sites: the A (Aminoacyl) site, the P (Peptidyl) site, and the E (Exit) site.
key_principles: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Initiation: In bacteria, the 16S rRNA 3' end base-pairs directly with the Shine-Dalgarno consensus (AGGAGG) upstream of the AUG start codon, positioning fMet-tRNA^fMet in the P site (assisted by IF1, IF2-GTP, IF3). In eukaryotes, the 43S pre-initiation complex (40S + eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi) binds the 5' m7G cap via eIF4F (eIF4E cap-binding + eIF4G scaffold + eIF4A helicase) and scans 5'->3' for the Kozak consensus (5'-GCCRCCAUGG-3').

The 3-Step Elongation Cycle (2 GTP per Peptide Bond): (1) Aminoacyl-tRNA Delivery: EF-Tu·GTP (eEF1A in eukaryotes) delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site; correct codon-anticodon geometry triggers 16S/18S rRNA decoding center rearrangement and GTP hydrolysis, releasing EF-Tu·GDP (regenerated by EF-Ts). (2) Peptidyl Transfer: The 23S/28S rRNA peptidyl transferase ribozyme catalyzes nucleophilic attack of the A-site α-amino group on the P-site ester carbonyl (0 GTP consumed directly). (3) Translocation: EF-G·GTP (eEF2 in eukaryotes, inhibited by Diphtheria toxin) hydrolyzes 1 GTP to shift the mRNA by 3 nucleotides, moving the deacylated tRNA to the E site and the peptidyl-tRNA from A to P.

Termination: Stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are recognized by protein Release Factors (RF1/RF2 + RF3-GTP in bacteria; eRF1 + eRF3-GTP in eukaryotes) that mimic tRNA shape and position a water molecule in the peptidyl transferase center to hydrolyze the finished polypeptide from the P-site tRNA.

sub_modules.title: Gene Regulation: Prokaryotic Operons, Eukaryotic Enhancers & Epigenetics
sub_modules.overview: Cells express only a fraction of their genome at any given moment, integrating environmental nutrient signals via prokaryotic operons and orchestrating cell-type identity via eukaryotic transcription factors and heritable epigenetic modifications.

core_concepts.heading: Prokaryotic Operon Logic: The lac and trp Operons
core_concepts.theory: Formulated by Jacob and Monod (1961), an operon is a polycistronic cluster of bacterial genes transcribed from a single promoter under the coordinate control of an Operator sequence and trans-acting regulatory proteins.
key_principles: The lac Operon (Dual Negative Inducible & Positive Catabolite Control): Encodes lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), and lacA (transacetylase). (1) Negative Control: In the absence of lactose, the LacI tetrameric repressor binds the Operator (O1/O2/O3), sterically blocking RNA Pol. Allolactose (or non-hydrolyzable IPTG) acts as an inducer, allosterically inactivating LacI. (2) Positive Control: Low glucose elevates cAMP via adenylate cyclase; cAMP binds CAP (CRP), which binds upstream of the promoter to bend DNA >90° and recruit RNA Pol (~50-fold activation).

The trp Operon (Negative Repressible & Ribosome Attenuation): Encodes 5 enzymes for tryptophan biosynthesis. (1) Repression: Tryptophan acts as a corepressor that binds the aporepressor TrpR, enabling it to bind the operator. (2) Attenuation: The 5' leader mRNA (trpL, regions 1–4) contains two tandem Trp codons. High Trp allows the ribosome to translate region 1 quickly, forcing regions 3 and 4 to base-pair into an intrinsic ρ-independent transcription terminator hairpin (followed by poly-U). Low Trp stalls the ribosome at the Trp codons, allowing the 2–3 anti-terminator hairpin to form so transcription proceeds.

core_concepts.heading: Eukaryotic Enhancer Looping, DNA Methylation & The Histone Code
core_concepts.theory: Eukaryotic genes are monocistronic and default to an 'OFF' state due to restrictive nucleosome packaging. Activation requires distal Enhancers looped to core promoters via the Mediator complex, alongside epigenetic writers, erasers, and readers.
key_principles: CpG Island DNA Methylation (Writers: DNMT1, DNMT3a/3b; Erasers: TET dioxygenases): Cytosine methylation at the C5 position (5-methylcytosine, 5mC) in promoter CpG islands recruits Methyl-CpG-Binding Domain (MBD/MeCP2) proteins and HDACs to silence transcription. DNMT1 maintains hemimethylated CpG sites after DNA replication.

Histone Tail Modifications (The Histone Code - Jenuwein & Allis): Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs, read by Bromodomains) acetylate lysine ε-amino groups (e.g., H3K9ac, H3K27ac), neutralizing the positive charge of lysine (+1 -> 0) to loosen DNA-histone electrostatic attraction and form transcriptionally active Euchromatin. Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) restore positive charge to condense chromatin.

Histone Methylation Valence (Read by Chromodomains & PHD Fingers): Unlike acetylation, lysine methylation does not alter charge; its effect depends on the exact residue: H3K4me3 marks active promoters, whereas H3K9me3 (bound by HP1 for constitutive heterochromatin) and H3K27me3 (deposited by PRC2 for facultative heterochromatin) drive transcriptional silencing.

solved_problems.title: DNA Topology & Supercoiling: Unwinding a Closed Circular Plasmid by Helicase & Topoisomerase Treatment
solved_problems.statement: A covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) plasmid in E. coli has a length of N = 5,250 base pairs. Assume B-DNA geometry with 10.5 base pairs per helical turn. (a) Calculate the relaxed linking number (Lk0) of this plasmid. (b) In vivo, DNA Gyrase maintains this plasmid at a negative superhelical density of σ = -0.060. Calculate the actual linking number (Lk) and linking number difference (ΔLk) of the isolated plasmid. (c) If a replication helicase unwinds (melts) 105 base pairs of this plasmid in the absence of topoisomerases, how does ΔTw and ΔWr change?

derivation_steps.explanation: Calculate the relaxed linking number (Lk0) by dividing total base pairs (N = 5,250 bp) by the helical repeat (h = 10.5 bp/turn):
Use the superhelical density equation (σ = ΔLk / Lk0) to solve for ΔLk and the actual integer Linking Number (Lk):
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \Delta Lk = \sigma \times Lk_0 = (-0.060)(500) = -30\text{ turns} \implies Lk = Lk_0 + \Delta Lk = 500 - 30 = 470

derivation_steps.explanation: When helicase melts 105 bp without breaking the phosphodiester backbone, Lk remains strictly constant (ΔLk_helicase = 0). Unwinding 105 bp decreases helical Twist by ΔTw = -105 / 10.5 = -10 turns:
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \Delta Lk_{\text{step}} = \Delta Tw + \Delta Wr = 0 \implies (-10) + \Delta Wr = 0 \implies \Delta Wr = +10\text{ supercoils}

derivation_steps.explanation: Add the +10 induced writhe to the initial writhe (-30) to find the net supercoiled state:
derivation_steps.equation_latex: Wr_{\text{final}} = -30 + 10 = -20\text{ negative supercoils (or if starting from relaxed DNA, +10 positive supercoils)}

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) Lk0 = 500 turns; (b) ΔLk = -30, Lk = 470; (c) Melting 105 bp decreases Twist by ΔTw = -10 and induces ΔWr = +10 positive supercoils (relaxing 10 of the 30 initial negative supercoils to leave Wr = -20).

solved_problems.title: Chromatin Compaction Ratio & Nucleosome Stoichiometry in a Human Chromosome
solved_problems.statement: Human Chromosome 12 contains approximately 1.32 × 10^8 base pairs (132 Mb) of linear B-DNA (0.34 nm rise per bp). During mitotic metaphase, Chromosome 12 is condensed into a rod-shaped structure measuring 4.5 μm in length. Assuming an average nucleosome repeat length of 200 bp (147 bp core DNA + 53 bp linker DNA): (a) Calculate the uncoiled contour length of Chromosome 12 DNA in millimeters. (b) Calculate the mitotic packing ratio (contour length / metaphase length). (c) Calculate the total number of nucleosomes and total number of individual core histone polypeptide molecules (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) bound to a single unreplicated (G1) Chromosome 12.

derivation_steps.explanation: Compute the linear contour length (L) of 1.32 × 10^8 bp of B-DNA (where 1 nm = 10^-6 mm):
Divide the linear contour length (44,880 μm) by the condensed metaphase chromosome length (4.5 μm) to obtain the packing ratio:
Divide total base pairs by the 200 bp repeat length to find the number of nucleosomes:
Since each nucleosome core octamer contains 8 core histone subunits (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4), multiply by 8:

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) Contour length = 44.88 mm; (b) Mitotic packing ratio ≈ 9,973:1 (~10,000-fold); (c) 6.60 × 10^5 nucleosomes and 5.28 × 10^6 core histone molecules.

solved_problems.title: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Replication Kinetics & Origin Density
solved_problems.statement: (a) The circular chromosome of E. coli contains 4.60 × 10^6 bp and replicates bidirectionally from a single origin (oriC). If each replication fork synthesizes DNA at v_fork = 1,000 bp/s, how many minutes are required to replicate the entire E. coli genome? (b) A diploid human cell contains 6.40 × 10^9 bp of nuclear DNA. In human cells, replication fork progression is much slower (v_fork = 50 bp/s) due to nucleosome disassembly/reassembly, yet S phase completes in 8.0 hours. Calculate the minimum number of bidirectional replication origins (N_origins) that must fire if all origins are active throughout the 8-hour S phase.

derivation_steps.explanation: For E. coli (1 origin = 2 bidirectional forks), the combined replication rate is 2 × 1,000 bp/s = 2,000 bp/s:
derivation_steps.equation_latex: t_{\text{E. coli}} = \frac{4.60 \times 10^6\text{ bp}}{2 \times 1,000\text{ bp/s}} = 2,300\text{ s} = \frac{2300}{60}\text{ min} = 38.33\text{ min}

derivation_steps.explanation: For the human diploid genome (G = 6.40 × 10^9 bp), convert S-phase duration (8.0 h) into seconds:
Calculate how many base pairs a single bidirectional origin (2 forks × 50 bp/s = 100 bp/s) can replicate in 28,800 s:

Divide the total diploid genome (6.40 × 10^9 bp) by the capacity of one origin (note: in vivo, origins fire asynchronously in clusters for ~1–2 h each, requiring ~30,000–50,000 total origins; this gives the theoretical minimum if active for the full 8 h):
derivation_steps.equation_latex: N_{\text{origins,min}} = \frac{6.40 \times 10^9\text{ bp}}{2.88 \times 10^6\text{ bp/origin}} = 2,222.2 \approx 2,223\text{ continuously active origins}

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) E. coli replication time = 38.3 min; (b) Minimum continuously active bidirectional origins = 2,223 (or ~17,780 origins if each replicon is active for 1 hour).

solved_problems.title: Energetic Cost & Coding Stoichiometry of Ribosomal Protein Synthesis
solved_problems.statement: A mature cytosolic enzyme in a bacterial cell has a molecular weight of 44,000 Da (44.0 kDa). Assuming the average molecular weight of an amino acid residue inside a polypeptide chain (after subtracting 18 Da for the H2O lost per peptide bond) is 110 Da, and the initiator formyl-methionine (fMet) was not cleaved post-translationally: (a) Calculate the exact number of amino acid residues (n) in the protein. (b) Calculate the minimum number of nucleotides in the mRNA open reading frame (including the start and stop codons). (c) Calculate the total number of high-energy phosphate bonds (~P equivalents from ATP and GTP) required to translate this polypeptide from free amino acids using the canonical 4n - 1 (and 4n with RF3-GTP) accounting.

derivation_steps.explanation: Divide the polypeptide molecular weight (44,000 Da) by the mean residue mass (110 Da/aa):
derivation_steps.equation_latex: n = \frac{44,000\text{ Da}}{110\text{ Da/aa}} = 400\text{ amino acid residues}

derivation_steps.explanation: Each of the 400 amino acids is encoded by a 3-nucleotide sense codon, plus 1 triplet stop codon (3 nt) that does not encode an amino acid:

Sum the high-energy phosphate bond equivalents: Aminoacyl-tRNA charging = 2n = 800 (~P from ATP -> AMP + 2 Pi); Initiation (IF2-GTP) = 1; Elongation A-site delivery (EF-Tu, n-1 cycles) = 399; Elongation translocation (EF-G, n-1 cycles) = 399:
derivation_steps.equation_latex: E_{4n-1} = 800 + 1 + 399 + 399 = 4(400) - 1 = 1,599\text{ high-energy phosphate bonds (or } 1,600\text{ if including 1 RF3-GTP at termination)}

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) n = 400 amino acids; (b) 1,203 nucleotides in the ORF; (c) 1,599 high-energy phosphate bonds (1,600 including RF3 termination GTP).

solved_problems.title: Transcriptional Kinetics: mRNA Half-Life & Steady-State Copy Number per Cell
solved_problems.statement: In an actively growing yeast cell, RNA Polymerase II initiates transcription of a metabolic gene at a constant rate of k_syn = 6.0 transcripts per minute. Upon addition of the transcription inhibitor 1,10-phenanthroline (or Actinomycin D), the cellular concentration of this mRNA drops to 12.5% (1/8) of its initial steady-state level in 15.0 minutes. Assuming first-order mRNA degradation kinetics: (a) Calculate the mRNA half-life (t_1/2) and the first-order decay constant (λ). (b) Calculate the steady-state number of mRNA molecules per cell ([mRNA]_ss) prior to inhibitor addition.

derivation_steps.explanation: Determine the number of half-lives elapsed when the mRNA fraction drops to 12.5% = 1/8 = (1/2)^3 in 15.0 minutes:
derivation_steps.equation_latex: \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^k = \frac{1}{8} \implies k = 3\text{ half-lives in } 15.0\text{ min} \implies t_{1/2} = \frac{15.0\text{ min}}{3} = 5.0\text{ min}

derivation_steps.explanation: Compute the first-order degradation rate constant λ from t_1/2 = ln(2) / λ:
At steady state, the synthesis rate equals the degradation rate (k_syn = λ [mRNA]_ss):

solved_problems.final_answer: (a) t_1/2 = 5.0 min, λ = 0.139 min^-1; (b) Steady-state abundance = 43 mRNA transcripts per cell.

practice_problems.question: Chemical analysis of a double-stranded viral genome reveals that 28% of its nitrogenous bases are Adenine (A). Assuming the genome obeys Chargaff's rules, calculate the molar percentages of Thymine (T), Guanine (G), and Cytosine (C), and determine the total GC content (%).
practice_problems.bold_answer: T = 28%, G = 22%, C = 22%; Total GC content = 44%
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: By Watson-Crick base pairing, %T = %A = 28%, so %A + %T = 56%. The remaining bases are G and C: %G + %C = 100% - 56% = 44% (total GC content). Since %G = %C, each comprises 44% / 2 = 22%.

practice_problems.question: In the Meselson-Stahl experiment, E. coli cells uniformly labeled for many generations in heavy 15N medium (15N/15N heavy DNA) are shifted to light 14N medium and allowed to undergo exactly 3 rounds of semiconservative replication. What fraction (percentage) of the resulting DNA duplex molecules will have intermediate hybrid density (15N/14N), and what fraction will have purely light density (14N/14N)?
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: After n = 3 generations from 1 parental 15N/15N duplex, there are 2^3 = 8 total DNA duplexes. Because the 2 original 15N single strands remain intact and each pairs with a newly synthesized 14N strand, there are always exactly 2 hybrid (15N/14N) duplexes. Thus, Hybrid = 2/8 = 25%, and Light (14N/14N) = 6/8 = 75%.

practice_problems.question: Consider an E. coli merodiploid (partial diploid) strain with the genotype: I^- P^+ O^c Z^- Y^+ / F' I^+ P^+ O^+ Z^+ Y^-. Predict whether β-galactosidase (LacZ) and β-galactoside permease (LacY) are synthesized constitutively, inducibly (only with lactose), or not at all.
practice_problems.bold_answer: LacZ (β-galactosidase) is Inducible; LacY (permease) is Constitutive
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: The F' episome carries a functional I+ gene encoding a diffusible trans-acting LacI repressor that binds wild-type O+ operators on both DNA molecules. On the chromosome, the O^c (operator-constitutive) mutation acts strictly in cis: it is linked to Z- (broken) and Y+ (functional), so Permease (LacY) is expressed constitutively regardless of lactose. On the F' plasmid, the functional Z+ gene is linked in cis to a wild-type O+ operator, so β-galactosidase (LacZ) is repressed in the absence of lactose and induced when lactose is added.

practice_problems.question: If a point mutation in a eukaryotic pre-mRNA changes the conserved 5' splice donor dinucleotide from 5'-GU-3' to 5'-AU-3' at the start of Intron 2 (located between Exon 2 of 120 nt and Exon 3 of 180 nt, with Intron 2 being 450 nt long containing an in-frame stop codon), what are the two most likely aberrant mature mRNA splicing outcomes?
practice_problems.bold_answer: Exon 2 Skipping (joining Exon 1 directly to Exon 3) or Intron 2 Retention (+450 nt leading to premature termination and Nonsense-Mediated Decay)
practice_problems.collapsible_derivation: Because U1 snRNA cannot base-pair with the mutated 5' splice donor site of Intron 2, the spliceosome either (1) skips Exon 2 entirely by pairing the 5' splice site of Intron 1 with the 3' splice site of Intron 2, or (2) fails to remove Intron 2 (intron retention), which introduces a Premature Termination Codon (PTC) >50 nt upstream of an Exon Junction Complex (EJC), targeting the transcript for Nonsense-Mediated mRNA Decay (NMD).

case_study.title: Pharmacogenomic & Epigenetic Case Study: Fluoroquinolone vs. Etoposide Topoisomerase Poisons & Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Cryptic Splicing
case_study.scenario: Case A: A patient with a urinary tract infection is treated with Ciprofloxacin, while an oncology patient receives Etoposide for small-cell lung cancer. Both drugs stabilize covalent Topoisomerase–DNA cleavage complexes. Case B: A child with Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) carries a de novo silent point mutation in codon 608 of the LMNA (Lamin A) gene (GGC -> GGT; Gly608Gly) that causes severe premature aging and nuclear envelope blebbing.
case_study.mechanistic_analysis: In Case A, Ciprofloxacin selectively poisons bacterial DNA Gyrase / Topoisomerase IV, whereas Etoposide poisons human Topoisomerase IIα. By trapping the covalent 5'-phosphotyrosyl enzyme-DNA intermediate after double-strand cleavage (preventing religation), advancing replication forks collide with the stalled complex, converting transient topological gates into lethal double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs). In Case B (HGPS), although GGC -> GGT is synonymous for Glycine, it activates a cryptic 5' splice donor site inside Exon 11 of pre-mRNA. The spliceosome excises 150 nucleotides from Exon 11, producing 'Progerin'—a mutant Lamin A lacking the ZMPSTE24 endoprotease cleavage site, leaving a permanent farnesyl lipid anchor that distorts the nuclear lamina.

quiz.question: Why does eukaryotic DNA replication require Telomerase at linear chromosome ends, whereas bacterial chromosomes do not?
options: Bacterial DNA Polymerase III can initiate synthesis de novo without an RNA primer

Removal of the terminal 5' RNA primer on the eukaryotic lagging strand leaves a 3' single-stranded overhang that cannot be filled because no upstream 3'-OH terminus exists; circular bacterial chromosomes always provide an upstream 3'-OH
Eukaryotic DNA Polymerases synthesize in the 3'->5' direction at telomeres
Telomerase is required to relieve positive supercoils ahead of the MCM2–7 helicase
quiz.explanation: All DNA polymerases require an upstream 3'-OH primer terminus to extend DNA in the 5'->3' direction. When the final RNA primer at the 5' end of a linear lagging strand is excised by RNase H / FEN1, there is no upstream 3'-OH to prime gap filling. Telomerase uses its internal RNA template (TERC) and reverse transcriptase (TERT) to elongate the 3' parental overhang so a new primer can be laid down.

quiz.question: How does Histone Acetyltransferase (HAT) activity directly promote transcriptional activation in eukaryotic chromatin?
options: It adds methyl groups to cytosine bases in promoter CpG islands

It transfers an acetyl group from Acetyl-CoA to the positively charged ε-amino group of histone tail lysines, neutralizing their +1 charge to weaken histone–DNA electrostatic binding and create binding sites for bromodomain remodelers
It cleaves Histone H1 via ubiquitin-proteasome degradation
It converts right-handed B-DNA into left-handed Z-DNA
quiz.explanation: At physiological pH, lysine side chains in histone tails carry a +1 charge that binds tightly to the negatively charged phosphodiester backbone of DNA. Acetylation converts the charged amine (-NH3+) into a neutral amide (-NH-CO-CH3), relaxing chromatin structure into open Euchromatin and recruiting bromodomain-containing coactivators.

quiz.question: During the first transesterification reaction of nuclear pre-mRNA splicing by the spliceosome, which chemical group acts as the nucleophile?
options: The 3'-OH group of the upstream exon (Exon 1)
The 2'-OH group of the conserved Branchpoint Adenine nucleotide within the intron
A free GTP cofactor bound to U1 snRNP
quiz.explanation: In Step 1 of nuclear pre-mRNA splicing, the 2'-OH of the intronic branchpoint adenosine attacks the 5' splice donor phosphodiester bond, forming a 2'-5' lariat intermediate and liberating the 3'-OH of Exon 1 (which then acts as the nucleophile in Step 2 to join the exons).

research_corner.paper_title: The Replication of DNA in Escherichia coli (Meselson & Stahl, 1958) & The Atomic Structure of the 50S Ribosomal Subunit (Ban, Nissen, Moore & Steitz, 2000)

imrad_breakdown.abstract_summary: Meselson and Stahl (1958) used equilibrium density-gradient centrifugation in CsCl to prove that DNA replicates semiconservatively rather than conservatively or dispersively. Ban & Steitz et al. (2000) solved the 2.4 Å crystal structure of the Haloarcula marismortui 50S ribosomal subunit, proving that the peptidyl transferase center is composed entirely of 23S rRNA.
imrad_breakdown.key_method: Isopycnic CsCl ultracentrifugation of 15N/14N DNA at 140,000 × g; X-ray crystallography using heavy-atom cluster phasing and transition-state analog inhibitors (CCdA-p-Puromycin).
imrad_breakdown.critical_takeaway: The ribosome is an ancient catalytic ribozyme (supporting the RNA World Hypothesis), where ribosomal proteins act primarily as peripheral architectural staples stabilizing the rRNA core.
